title: Short Stuff: Lying in State
summary: Short Stuff episode on lying in state, prompted by the death of Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who was set to become the first woman to lie in state in the US Capitol Rotunda. The hosts explain that Congress decides whether someone lies in state (by resolution or leadership agreement), that presidents and ex-presidents are automatically offered it, and that the Architect of the Capitol prepares the Rotunda. They cover the catafalque (originally built for Lincoln in 1865), the first lying in state (Henry Clay, 1852), recent honorees (John McCain, Elijah Cummings, John Lewis, Rosa Parks as a private citizen in 2005), and the difference between lying in state and lying in repose. Families of Truman and Nixon declined the honor, and Ginsburg lay in repose at the Supreme Court. An anthropologist's view that these ceremonies "embalm an idea" of national spirit is also discussed.

segments.title: Ginsburg's death and the first lying in state
segments.summary: Hosts note Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's death and that she will be the first woman to lie in state at the Capitol. They describe the solemn purpose of lying in state and its history, including Henry Clay in 1852, and list recent honorees such as McCain, Cummings, Lewis and Rosa Parks.

segments.title: Who decides and who is eligible
segments.summary: Congress decides whether someone lies in state, usually by resolution or leadership agreement. Presidents and ex-presidents are automatically offered the honor; others need Congress's approval. Private citizens rarely receive it, and lying in honor is a different honor.

segments.title: Preparing the Capitol and the catafalque
segments.summary: The Architect of the Capitol is notified and prepares the building with cleaning, power washing and polishing. The coffin rests on a catafalque, often the one first built for Abraham Lincoln in 1865. Families may decline the honor, as Truman's and Nixon's did, and lying in repose is the non-state version.

segments.title: Purpose of the ceremony and Ginsburg's repose
segments.summary: Ginsburg lies in repose at the Supreme Court after her family declined lying in state. The hosts describe the Rotunda setup for media and ceremony. Anthropologist Shannon Lee Doughty's view is that these ceremonies embalm an idea of national spirit and unite the country.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the episode with closing remarks and the show credit.
